name: Hadean
desc: The Earth forms from dust and rock around the young Sun. A planet about the size of Mars crashes into it, and the debris becomes the Moon. By 4.4 billion years ago there is liquid water — but almost no rock from this time survives.
funFact: The oldest pieces of the Earth you could hold are tiny crystals called zircons from the Jack Hills of Australia: 4.4 billion years old, older than any rock.
lifeNote: No sure sign of life is known from the Hadean: almost no rock survives from it. A speck of carbon inside a 4.1-billion-year-old crystal may be a trace of life — that is argued over.

insight.big: The Earth is born, the Moon is made, and the first oceans form — almost nothing survives to show us.
signs: The first solid grains of the Solar System form around the young Sun; the Earth grows from them.
A planet about the size of Mars hits the young Earth, and the debris gathers into the Moon. This is the best-supported idea; exactly how it happened is argued over.
Crystals from Australia show there was already liquid water — and perhaps the first continental crust.
No rock from the Hadean survives in place, so nobody knows where any land was. The map shows only the sea.
insight.know: Zircon crystals survive almost anything. The uranium in them turns into lead at a known rate, so they keep their age, and the oxygen in them shows whether they formed near liquid water.
insight.today: The Moon made in that collision raises our tides today, and its pull has been slowing the Earth’s spin ever since.

name: Eoarchean
desc: The oldest rocks that survive form in this time, in north-west Canada. Life may already be here: Greenland holds 3.7-billion-year-old cone shapes that some scientists read as the oldest fossils.
funFact: The Acasta Gneiss, in Canada’s Northwest Territories, is about 4 billion years old — the oldest rock known on Earth.

insight.big: The oldest rocks — and perhaps the oldest signs of life.
signs: The oldest rock known: the Acasta Gneiss, in north-west Canada.
Small cone shapes in Greenland may be the oldest stromatolites, built by microbes — or folds in the rock. Argued over.
A world ocean, and almost no oxygen in the air.
Where land stood is unknown; the map shows only the sea.
insight.know: Rocks this old have been squeezed and heated many times. Finding life in them means telling shapes made by microbes from shapes made by folding — which is why the Greenland cones are still argued over.
insight.today: If life appeared soon after the oceans formed, scientists ask, does it arise easily wherever conditions allow?

name: Paleoarchean
desc: Microbes build mound-shaped reefs — stromatolites — in shallow seas and around hot springs in what is now Western Australia. These are among the oldest widely accepted signs of life.
funFact: Stromatolites are still being built today, at Shark Bay in Western Australia — the same corner of the world as the 3.5-billion-year-old ones.

insight.big: Microbes build reefs: the oldest widely accepted signs of life.
signs: A reef of stromatolites of many shapes at Strelley Pool, Australia — built by microbes.
Hot springs on land in the Pilbara hold signs of microbial life: perhaps life on land already.
Microbial mats on land, beside rivers, in South Africa.
insight.know: A stromatolite grows in layers as microbes trap sand and build on top of one another. Its wavy, cone and dome shapes, and chemical traces inside the layers, are hard to make without life.
insight.today: Stromatolites were the main sign of life you could see for most of Earth’s history.

name: Mesoarchean
desc: Microbial mats cover shores and riverbanks. Traces in ancient soils suggest living things were already making a little oxygen, about 3 billion years ago — long before it built up in the air.
funFact: The oxygen you breathe was first made by microbes. Traces in 3-billion-year-old soils in South Africa may be the first hint of them at work.
lifeNote: No fossil on this site is dated to this time. The best signs of life are microbial mats and chemical traces, too small to name.

insight.big: A first hint of oxygen made by living things.
signs: Traces in ancient soil in South Africa suggest a little oxygen in the air, made by microbes — if the reading is right.
The deep sea is full of dissolved iron, with no oxygen.
Microbial mats on shores and tidal flats.
insight.know: Chromium in soil only moves about when there is oxygen. Its traces in old soils, and in mud laid down nearby, are read as a sign that oxygen existed.
insight.today: Every breath you take depends on what microbes started in seas like these.

name: Neoarchean
desc: Oxygen-making microbes spread, and brief “whiffs” of oxygen come and go a few hundred million years before it builds up for good. Striped rocks of iron settle on the sea floor.
funFact: Striped rocks of iron and silica — banded iron formations — were laid down on the sea floor in this time: iron in the sea rusting out as the first oxygen appeared.
lifeNote: No fossil on this site is dated to this time. Life is everywhere in the shallow seas, but as mats and chemical traces rather than named fossils.

insight.big: Oxygen-making microbes spread; oxygen comes and goes in brief whiffs.
signs: A brief whiff of oxygen, before the big rise.
Striped iron rocks — banded iron formations — build up on the sea floor.
insight.know: Some metals, like molybdenum, wash off the land only when oxygen weathers the rocks. A short pulse of them in 2.5-billion-year-old mud is read as a whiff of oxygen.
insight.today: The oxygen in today’s air began as a waste gas of microbes like these.

name: Siderian
desc: The Great Oxidation Event: oxygen builds up in the air for the first time. The Earth also goes through some of its first great ice ages.
funFact: Before this time a pile of iron sand left out in the air would not have rusted: there was no oxygen in the air to rust it.
lifeNote: No fossil on this site is dated to this time. The microbes that made the oxygen are known from the chemistry of the rocks, not from named fossils.

insight.big: The Great Oxidation Event: oxygen in the air, for good.
signs: Oxygen builds up in the air for the first time — the Great Oxidation Event.
Some of the Earth’s first great ice ages.
Microbes, including the oxygen-makers; for many others oxygen was a poison.
insight.know: Before the rise of oxygen, sulfur in rocks kept an unusual chemical signature that only an air without oxygen allows. It vanishes at the Great Oxidation Event, which dates it.
insight.today: Oxygen was a poison to many microbes of the time; it also made later animals, including us, possible.

name: Rhyacian
desc: Oxygen stays in the air. In Gabon, 2.1-billion-year-old rocks hold centimetre-sized fossils that some scientists think were early many-celled life — far older than any other.
funFact: The Francevillian fossils from Gabon look like flat, wrinkled pancakes up to 12 cm across.

insight.big: Oxygen stays — and perhaps a first try at large life.
signs: The Francevillian fossils of Gabon: flat, lobed shapes up to 12 cm across. Early many-celled life — or shapes made by microbes? Argued over.
In the air to stay, though far below today’s level.
insight.know: X-ray scans of the Gabon fossils show they were three-dimensional and grew in a regular way — why some scientists think they were living things, not mineral shapes.
insight.today: If the Gabon fossils were alive, large life had a first try more than a billion years before it took hold.

name: Orosirian
desc: The biggest known asteroid crater on Earth, Vredefort, is made in what is now South Africa. In Ontario, microbes are sealed in glassy rock so well that their shapes can still be seen. The pieces of Nuna begin to gather.
funFact: The Vredefort crater in South Africa, about 2 billion years old, is the largest asteroid crater known on Earth.

insight.big: The biggest known crater, the clearest early microbes, and the start of Nuna.
signs: A huge asteroid strikes what is now South Africa, leaving the Vredefort crater — the largest known.
The Gunflint microbes of Ontario, among the first fossils ever recognised from this far back, described in 1965.
Collisions begin to gather land into the supercontinent Nuna.
Where land stood is unknown until 1.8 billion years ago.
insight.know: Chert, a glassy rock made of silica, can seal microbes in before they rot. Thin slices of the Gunflint chert show threads and tiny spheres.
insight.today: The Gunflint fossils showed that life had a long history before the Cambrian — an answer to Darwin’s puzzle about the missing early fossils.

name: Statherian
desc: Most of the land gathers into an older supercontinent, Nuna (also called Columbia). The air holds only a little oxygen, the land is bare, and life is microscopic — until the first living things made of many cells appear in the sea.
funFact: A day lasted about 19 hours — and scientists think it stayed that long for a billion years, while the pull of the Moon and the Sun’s warming of the air balanced each other out.

insight.big: An older supercontinent, Nuna, and the first living things made of many cells.
signs: Most of the land gathers into a supercontinent, Nuna (also called Columbia), around what is now North America. The map shows one model of it; the details are argued over.
Only a little oxygen — far less than today.
About 19 hours, and it stayed about that long for a billion years.
Chains of cells 1.63 billion years old in northern China: some of the oldest living things made of many cells.
insight.know: Rocks this old are mostly worn away or buried. A supercontinent is pieced together from mountain belts of the same age on different continents, and from the magnetism frozen into old lava, which tells how far from the poles each piece lay.
insight.today: Life spent well over a billion years as single cells and small threads before anything large evolved. Most of Earth’s history belongs to microbes.

name: Calymmian
desc: Living things big enough to see with your own eyes: ribbons of seaweed up to 30 cm long grow on the sea floor in what is now China. Everything else is still microscopic.
funFact: The oldest living things big enough to see without a microscope are seaweed-like ribbons about 1.56 billion years old.

insight.big: Seaweeds you could see — and cells with spines and ridges, built to survive.
signs: Ribbons up to 30 cm long, 1.56 billion years old, in the Gaoyuzhuang rocks of China: many-celled seaweeds, big enough to see.
Cells in 1.6-billion-year-old rocks in India look like red seaweeds. If they are, they are the oldest; many scientists are not convinced.
Single cells with walls covered in spines and ridges float in the sea: complex cells, not bacteria.
Still very little oxygen in the air, and almost none in the deep sea.
insight.know: Microscopic fossils are freed from the rock with acid. Their walls — decorated with spines, ridges or branches — show they were complex cells with a nucleus, not bacteria.
insight.today: The seaweeds and the green plants that came from them belong to lines whose first members turn up in rocks like these.

name: Ectasian
desc: The middle of what geologists call the “boring billion”: the climate, the sea and life change only slowly. There is little oxygen in the air — though some seas have enough for animals, which have not evolved.
funFact: Rocks in northern China show that, 1.4 billion years ago, some seas had enough oxygen for animals to breathe — but there were no animals yet. Something else was missing.
lifeNote: No fossil on this site is dated to these 200 million years. Rocks this old are scarce, and the microbes in them are hard to tell apart — life was there, but none of it has a name here yet.

insight.big: The “boring billion”: little oxygen, slow change — and a puzzle about why animals did not appear.
signs: Low in the air overall, but in some shallow seas enough for animals to breathe — with no animals to breathe it.
Almost no oxygen in the deep ocean.
Microbes, single-celled algae with decorated walls, and small seaweeds.
insight.know: Some metals, like chromium, behave differently when there is oxygen around. Their traces in old sea-floor mud tell how much oxygen there was in the air and the water.
insight.today: Oxygen alone does not make animals. Why complex life took so long, after the air and sea could support it, is still a big open question.

name: Stenian
desc: Pieces of land crash together to build Rodinia, raising a long mountain belt down the east side of North America. In the sea, red seaweeds appear — and with them, perhaps, the oldest known sex.
funFact: Nori, the seaweed wrapped round sushi, is a red alga — a distant relative of Bangiomorpha, which lived 1.05 billion years ago.

insight.big: Rodinia is built, and red seaweeds appear — perhaps with the oldest known sex.
signs: Collisions build the supercontinent Rodinia, raising a mountain belt (the Grenville) down the east side of North America.
Bangiomorpha, a red seaweed about 1.05 billion years old from Arctic Canada — the oldest seaweed we can match to a group alive today.
Microscopic life in lakes in Scotland, about a billion years old: the first known life away from the sea.
insight.know: Bangiomorpha’s threads made different kinds of spore, as living red seaweeds with male and female forms do. Dating the rock layers around it put it at about 1.05 billion years.
insight.today: Nori, the seaweed on sushi, is one of its distant relatives.

name: Tonian
desc: Much of the land gathers into a supercontinent, Rodinia, around North America — and later starts to break apart. The land is bare rock and sand: nothing grows on it. In the sea live microbes, seaweeds, the first fungi, and perhaps the first sponges.
funFact: A day lasted only about 19 to 21 hours, because the Earth was spinning faster. The Moon’s pull has been slowing it down ever since.

insight.big: A billion years ago: a supercontinent gathering, bare land, and life still tiny — but the first seaweeds, fungi and perhaps sponges are here.
signs: Much of the land gathers into a supercontinent, Rodinia, with North America at its heart; it begins to tear apart about 800 to 750 million years ago. Which pieces belonged to it, and where each one sat, is argued over — the map shows one model.
No plants and no animals on land: bare rock and sand.
About 19 hours at the start, getting longer: the Moon’s pull slows the Earth’s spin.
Green seaweeds a billion years old, the oldest known fungi, and amoebae living in tiny vase-shaped shells.
Tangled tubes in 890-million-year-old reefs may be the first sponges — the oldest animals, if they are right.
insight.know: There are no bones or shells yet. The fossils are single cells and threads, found by dissolving rock in acid or slicing it thin and looking through a microscope. Chemical tests on the cell walls tell a fungus from a seaweed.
insight.today: The branch of life that holds every plant, fungus and animal alive today was spreading through these seas. Fungi are closer cousins of animals than plants are.

name: Cryogenian
desc: Snowball Earth! The entire planet freezes over, with ice covering even the equator. Strange and terrifying, but life persists.
funFact: Snowball Earth was probably triggered by a combination of continental movement and volcanic activity. The planet was a frozen wasteland for millions of years before finally thawing.

insight.big: Earth froze almost solid — twice — and life came through it.
signs: Two “Snowball Earth” ice ages: the Sturtian (about 717–660 MYA) and the Marinoan (about 650–635 MYA). Glaciers reached sea level at the equator.
Very little oxygen. Carbon dioxide from volcanoes built up for millions of years under the ice — until the greenhouse grew strong enough to melt it.
About 21.9 hours. A year had roughly 400 days.
Microbes, algae and probably the first sponges, surviving in open cracks, meltwater pools and around volcanic vents.
insight.know: Rocks dropped by melting icebergs lie in sea-floor mud whose magnetic grains show it formed near the equator. Directly on top sit “cap carbonates” — limestone laid down fast as the ice vanished into a hothouse.
insight.today: Snowball Earth is the clearest case of a climate feedback running away: ice reflects sunlight, which cools the planet, which makes more ice. It also shows that a greenhouse atmosphere can end even a frozen world.

name: Ediacaran
desc: The ice melts — and the first large, complex living things appear. Soft-bodied fronds, discs and quilted mats carpet the sea floor: a strange garden with no eyes, no jaws and no legs.
funFact: Ediacaran creatures were so unlike anything alive today that scientists argued for decades about whether they were animals, giant single cells, lichens — or a failed experiment in life that left no descendants at all.

insight.big: Life gets large — soft, strange, and unlike anything alive today.
signs: Warming after Snowball Earth, with one brief ice age (the Gaskiers, about 580 MYA).
Oxygen reaches the deep ocean for the first time — possibly what allowed big bodies to evolve.
The southern continents are colliding to assemble Gondwana.
Fronds, discs and quilted mats up to 2 m long. By the end: the first burrows, the first shells — and the first holes drilled in them by predators.
insight.know: Ediacaran organisms had no bones or shells; they survive as impressions pressed into sand and volcanic ash at Mistaken Point (Canada), the Ediacara Hills (Australia) and the White Sea (Russia). In 2018, fossil cholesterol recovered from one of them, Dickinsonia, showed it was an animal.
insight.today: Named in 2004, the Ediacaran was the first new geological period to be declared in 120 years. Its fossils record life's first experiment with being big.

name: Cambrian
desc: The ocean EXPLODES with life! Almost every type of animal body plan appears for the very first time — it's like evolution tried all its best ideas at once.
funFact: Before the Cambrian, most life was just blobs and thin mats. Then in about 20 million years, eyes, claws, shells, fins, and legs all appeared at once! Scientists call this the Cambrian Explosion.

insight.big: In a geological blink, nearly every major animal body plan appears.
signs: A warm greenhouse world with no ice at the poles.
Many times today's level — rough estimates run to 10–20 times.
High and rising. Warm, shallow seas spread across the continents.
Bare rock and crusts of microbes. No plants, no animals on land.
insight.know: Two exceptional fossil beds — the Burgess Shale in Canada and Chengjiang in China — were buried so fast in fine mud that eyes, guts, gills and legs survive, not just shells. Charles Walcott, Secretary of the Smithsonian, found the Burgess Shale in 1909 and collected about 65,000 specimens, still held in Washington.
insight.today: Your own body plan — a head end, paired eyes, a nerve cord along the back — goes back to small Cambrian swimmers like Pikaia.

name: Ordovician
desc: Seas fill with extraordinary creatures — giant nautiloids, sea scorpions, strange jawless fish. Then Earth's continents drift over the South Pole, causing an ice age that kills 85% of all species.
funFact: The whole period ends when South America and Africa drift over the South Pole! The oceans freeze, sea levels drop, and 85% of species go extinct. One of the Big Five mass extinctions.
event: End-Ordovician Extinction: Ice age wipes out 85% of all species when the continents drift over the South Pole!

insight.big: Life in the sea triples in variety — then an ice age brings the first of the “Big Five” mass extinctions.
signs: A hot greenhouse that cools into a short, severe ice age at the very end (about 445–443 MYA).
Among the highest of the last 540 million years — then a fall of 50–100 m as the ice grew.
The first plants: moss-like and tiny, known only from their spores, about 470 MYA.
Gondwana drifts across the South Pole.
insight.know: Bedrock in today's Sahara is scratched and polished by glaciers of this age: North Africa was then at the South Pole. And microscopic spores in 470-million-year-old rock are the first sign of plants on land, long before any plant body is preserved.
insight.today: It is proof that cooling can kill as thoroughly as warming. What matters is how fast the climate changes.

ext.name: End-Ordovician mass extinction
ext.cause: A short, intense ice age. Sea level fell, shallow seas drained and the water chilled; a second wave of extinction followed as the ice melted and oxygen-poor water spread.

name: Silurian
desc: Life bounces back! The FIRST jawed fish appear — a game-changing invention. For the very first time, plants creep onto land. Sea scorpions reach their peak size.
funFact: Jaws were one of the most important evolutionary inventions ever. Before jaws: you can only filter or suck food. With jaws: you can bite, chew, hunt anything. Everything changes!

insight.big: Life recovers — and takes its first firm steps onto land.
signs: Warm and stable once the ice melts; the seas rise again.
The first upright plants with water-carrying tubes, a few centimetres tall. The first land animals: millipedes and relatives of spiders.
Vast reefs of corals and sponges. The first fish with jaws.
Oxygen is climbing: the oldest charcoal — the first wildfire — dates to about 420 MYA.
Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia collide, raising the mountains of Scotland and Scandinavia.
insight.know: Fossil Cooksonia stems from Wales and Ireland preserve the earliest water-conducting cells. Charcoal proves fire — and fire needs both land plants to burn and air that is at least about 16% oxygen.
insight.today: Every forest, field and garden descends from these finger-high pioneers. Plants on land also began making the first soils and pulling CO₂ out of the air.

name: Devonian
desc: The AGE OF FISH! Giant armored fish rule the seas. Enormous forests cover the land. And then... fish grow legs and start crawling onto land. Every land animal alive today is descended from them.
funFact: A fish growing legs and walking onto land is one of the most important moments in the history of ALL land animals. Every amphibian, reptile, dinosaur, bird, and mammal — including you — descends from those brave fish.
event: Late Devonian Extinction: 75% of species lost. The giant armored fish disappear forever.

insight.big: The Age of Fishes — and of the first forests, the first seeds and the first four-legged animals.
signs: Falls steeply as the first forests and deep soils lock carbon away.
From ankle-high plants to trees 30 m tall in about 50 million years.
About 22 hours — roughly 400 days in a year.
Some of the largest reefs in Earth history; one still stands as limestone ranges in Western Australia.
insight.know: Devonian corals laid down one growth line a day. Counting them in 1963, John Wells found about 400 lines per year — so each day was about 22 hours long. Earth's spin has been slowing ever since, braked by the Moon's tides.
insight.today: The bones of your arm — one bone, two bones, lots of little bones, then fingers — were laid out in Devonian fishes such as Tiktaalik.

ext.name: Late Devonian mass extinction
ext.when: About 372 MYA, with a second crisis about 359 MYA
ext.toll: About 70–75% of species; reef builders and armoured fishes were hit hardest
ext.cause: Still debated. Leading ideas: oceans starved of oxygen — possibly fed by nutrients washing off newly forested land — together with climate cooling and volcanism.

name: Carboniferous
desc: Enormous swampy forests cover the land. Oxygen levels soar so high that GIANT insects fill the air. The first reptiles appear — able to lay eggs on dry land for the first time ever.
funFact: Oxygen was 35% of the air — way higher than today's 21%! Insects breathe through tubes, not lungs, so more oxygen = bigger insects. That's why there were dragonflies with 70cm wingspans.

insight.big: Coal forests bury so much carbon that the air fills with oxygen and the planet slides into an ice age.
signs: Up to about 30–35% of the air (21% today) — the highest ever. Giant insects follow.
Falls to levels close to today's.
Tropical coal swamps at the equator; great ice sheets over the southern continents.
Rises and falls by tens of metres as the ice sheets grow and melt.
Laurussia and Gondwana collide to begin building Pangaea, raising the Appalachians.
insight.know: Coal seams are those forests, compressed. Repeating stacks of coal, shale and limestone record the sea rising and falling in step with the ice — in the same orbital rhythm that paced our own Ice Age.
insight.today: Much of the coal that powered the Industrial Revolution formed in these swamps. Burning it returns to the air, in a few centuries, carbon that took millions of years to bury.

name: Permian
desc: All continents fuse into one giant supercontinent — PANGAEA. Sail-backed synapsids rule the land. These 'mammal-like reptiles' are YOUR ancestors. Then comes THE GREAT DYING...
funFact: The Permian ends with the worst extinction in Earth's entire history. Volcanoes in Siberia flood an area the size of a continent with lava, pumping out greenhouse gases that overheat the planet and strip the oceans of oxygen. Around nine in ten ocean species vanish.
event: ⚠️ THE GREAT DYING: around nine in ten ocean species and seven in ten land vertebrates wiped out — the worst extinction in Earth's history, driven by colossal volcanic eruptions in Siberia.

insight.big: One supercontinent, one world ocean — and the worst extinction of all time.
signs: Pangaea stretches almost from pole to pole.
An ice age at the start; hot, dry interior deserts by the end.
Synapsids — the line that leads to mammals — rule the land.
A single ocean, Panthalassa, with the Tethys Sea cutting into Pangaea's eastern side.
insight.know: A layer of volcanic ash at Meishan, China, dates the extinction to within tens of thousands of years — and it lines up with the eruption of the Siberian Traps. Earlier in the Permian, identical fossils (the reptile Mesosaurus, the plant Glossopteris) on continents now oceans apart were key evidence for continental drift.
insight.today: It is the best-studied example of what a rapid release of greenhouse gas does to the sea: warming, acidification and loss of oxygen — the same three changes now being measured in today's oceans.

ext.name: End-Permian mass extinction — “the Great Dying”
ext.when: About 251.9 MYA, over roughly 60,000 years or less
ext.toll: Roughly 80–95% of marine species and about 70% of land vertebrates; the only known mass extinction of insects
ext.cause: Eruption of the Siberian Traps, one of the largest volcanic events known. CO₂ and other gases drove around 10 °C of warming, acidified the oceans and drained them of oxygen.

name: Triassic
desc: Life rebuilds on a scorching Pangaea. The FIRST dinosaurs appear — small, fast, humble. Pterosaurs take to the air! Ichthyosaurs return to the sea. Tiny mammals scurry in the shadows.
funFact: The first dinosaurs weren't giants — they were small, fast runners about the size of a dog! It took tens of millions of years before they grew into the giants we know. Slow and steady wins the evolutionary race.
event: End-Triassic Extinction: Massive volcanic eruptions split Pangaea and wipe out 76% of species — clearing the way for dinosaurs to dominate!

insight.big: Life restarts from near zero — and dinosaurs, mammals, turtles, crocodile-relatives and pterosaurs all appear.
signs: Hot and dry with no polar ice. In the first few million years, tropical seas reached about 40 °C — too hot for most life.
About 234–232 MYA it rained, on and off, for one to two million years. Dinosaurs diversified straight afterwards.
Forests took so long to return that no coal formed anywhere on Earth for millions of years.
Pangaea is whole — and begins to tear apart at the very end.
insight.know: The oldest well-dated dinosaurs come from Argentina and southern Brazil, where layers of volcanic ash give precise ages of about 233–231 million years. They were small, two-legged and rare: a minor part of a world run by other reptiles.
insight.today: The bird line and the crocodile line split here. Birds and crocodiles are still each other's closest living relatives.

ext.name: End-Triassic mass extinction
ext.toll: About three-quarters of species, including most of the big crocodile-line reptiles
ext.cause: Vast eruptions (the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province) as Pangaea split open where the Atlantic is today, releasing CO₂ that warmed the planet and acidified the oceans. The same lavas form the Palisades cliffs across the river from New York City.

name: Jurassic
desc: The age of GIANTS! Pangaea splits apart. The world is warm and lush. Sauropods reach impossible sizes. Stegosaurus roams, Allosaurus hunts. And the very first birds take flight.
funFact: Some of the longest animals EVER to walk on land lived in the Jurassic! Supersaurus reached about 33–35 meters — longer than a blue whale, though far lighter. (The heaviest land animals of all, the titanosaurs, came later, in the Cretaceous.)

insight.big: Pangaea breaks in two, the Atlantic is born, and dinosaurs become giants.
signs: Warm and humid, with little or no polar ice.
Forests of conifers, cycads, ginkgoes and ferns. No flowers. No grass.
High — shallow seas flood much of Europe.
Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south separate; the central Atlantic opens from about 175 MYA.
insight.know: The Morrison Formation of the western USA — river and floodplain muds about 156–147 million years old — has yielded Allosaurus, Stegosaurus, Diplodocus and many more from the same layers, which is how we know they lived side by side.
insight.today: Plankton-rich mud from Jurassic seas became much of the world's oil, including the fields of the North Sea and Saudi Arabia.

name: Cretaceous
desc: Dinosaurs THRIVE in tropical seas and steamy jungles. New flowering plants emerge. Tyrannosaurus appears — the largest land predator ever. Then a space rock changes everything in an instant.
funFact: An asteroid about 10 km wide hits Earth at around 20 km per second. The blast is roughly a million times more powerful than the biggest nuclear bomb ever tested. About three-quarters of all species vanish — including every dinosaur except the birds.
event: ⚠️ K–Pg EXTINCTION: An asteroid slams into Earth! Dinosaurs die — but birds survive and thrive. Mammals inherit the world.

insight.big: A hothouse world of flowering plants, giant dinosaurs and high seas — ended in a day by an asteroid.
signs: One of the warmest times of the last 500 million years, peaking about 90 MYA. Forests and dinosaurs lived near both poles.
Perhaps 100–250 m higher than today. A seaway split North America in two.
Around 1,000 parts per million or more (today: about 425).
Flowering plants appear about 130 MYA and take over. Bees, ants, snakes and modern bird groups arrive.
South America and Africa part; India breaks away and races north.
insight.know: A thin layer of clay found all over the world is rich in iridium — rare in Earth's crust, common in asteroids (Luis and Walter Alvarez, 1980). The same layer holds shocked quartz and beads of melted rock. The buried crater, 180 km across, was identified at Chicxulub, Mexico, in 1991.
insight.today: Birds are living dinosaurs — about 11,000 species of them. And the asteroid shows that the dominant animals of an age can vanish quickly, opening the way for others: in this case mammals, and eventually us.

ext.name: End-Cretaceous (K–Pg) mass extinction
ext.toll: About 75% of species, including every dinosaur except the birds
ext.cause: An asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Yucatán. Soot and dust blocked the Sun and stopped photosynthesis for months to years. Enormous eruptions in India (the Deccan Traps) were already under way and may have added to the stress.

name: Paleogene
desc: The age of BIRDS and MAMMALS! Dinosaurs are dead, and the small furry creatures that hid for 150 million years now explode in diversity. Giant flightless birds rule some continents.
funFact: Without dinosaurs in the way, mammals went WILD with evolution. In just 10 million years, they filled every role dinosaurs once held. Some got huge (like Indricotherium, bigger than any land animal today). Life adapts incredibly fast.

insight.big: Mammals and birds inherit the Earth, and the climate swings from extreme hothouse to the first Antarctic ice.
signs: A sudden release of carbon warmed the planet by 5–8 °C in under 20,000 years. The heat lasted about 200,000 years.
Palm trees and alligator relatives live in the Arctic. CO₂ is above 1,000 parts per million.
CO₂ has fallen; Antarctica freezes over for the first time in over 200 million years.
Tens of metres higher than today until the ice sheets form.
India collides with Asia (about 50 MYA) and the Himalayas begin to rise.
insight.know: The shells of microscopic sea creatures record ocean temperature in their chemistry. Cores drilled from the sea floor give an unbroken temperature record for the whole of the last 66 million years.
insight.today: The warming 56 million years ago is the closest natural parallel to our own — but carbon is entering the air today about ten times faster than it did then.

name: Neogene
desc: Grasslands spread as forests decline. Mammals specializing in running and grazing appear. Apes evolve in Africa. Mammoths appear, saber-tooths sharpen their fangs, and humans emerge.
funFact: Climate change — caused by continental positions and ocean currents — transformed Earth's landscape. Tropical jungles gave way to grasslands, changing what animals could survive.

insight.big: Grasslands spread, apes flourish — and one line of apes stands up.
signs: A long cooling. Antarctic ice expands about 14 MYA; ice forms in the Arctic by about 3 MYA.
Tropical grasses spread 8–6 MYA, creating the savannas.
About 5.97–5.33 MYA the Mediterranean was cut off from the Atlantic and nearly evaporated, leaving salt over a kilometre thick.
The Isthmus of Panama joins the Americas by about 3 MYA; animals walk both ways.
DNA puts the split between the human line and the chimpanzee line at roughly 7–6 MYA.
insight.know: Tooth enamel records what an animal ate. The carbon in fossil teeth from Pakistan to Kenya shifts between 8 and 6 million years ago, tracking grazing animals as they switched from forest leaves to tropical grass.
insight.today: About 3 million years ago CO₂ was close to today's level, the world was 2–3 °C warmer and the seas were perhaps 10–20 m higher. It is studied as a preview of where today's atmosphere leads once oceans and ice sheets catch up.

name: Quaternary
desc: Ice sheets swallow half the world. Woolly mammoths, cave lions, and giant ground sloths roam the frozen lands. Homo sapiens appear and quickly spread to every corner of the planet.
funFact: Woolly mammoths were still alive on a remote Arctic island when the ancient Egyptians were building the Great Pyramid. The last ones died only about 4,000 years ago — and why they finally vanished is still debated.
event: Megafauna Extinction: Humans spread across the globe and the great Ice Age mammals start vanishing — mammoths, ground sloths, cave lions, all gone.
title: Ice Age

insight.big: The Ice Age: glaciers advance and retreat dozens of times while the human family spreads across the world.
signs: About 50 cold–warm cycles: every 41,000 years at first, then roughly every 100,000 years.
The last peak of the ice. The world averaged about 6 °C colder; ice up to 3 km thick covered Canada and Scandinavia.
About 120 m lower at glacial peaks. Land bridges joined Siberia to Alaska, Britain to Europe, and New Guinea to Australia.
Swings between about 180 parts per million (cold) and 280 (warm).
insight.know: Ice drilled from Antarctica holds bubbles of ancient air: a direct sample of the atmosphere going back 800,000 years. Cores recovered in 2025 reach back more than a million.
insight.today: Earth's orbit sets the rhythm of the ice ages; CO₂ amplifies it. Today's CO₂ — above 420 parts per million — is higher than at any point in the ice-core record.

ext.name: The loss of the giants
ext.toll: Most large mammals outside Africa: about 70% of the big-mammal groups of North America, over 80% in South America and nearly 90% in Australia
ext.cause: Debated: hunting by modern humans as they spread, rapid climate change at the end of the last ice age, or both together. The losses follow the arrival of people — Australia first, the Americas later, islands like Madagascar and New Zealand last.

name: Holocene
desc: All of recorded human history — ancient Egypt, Rome, the Middle Ages, today — fits into less than 0.002% of the time life has existed on Earth. We are the newest chapter.
funFact: If all of Earth's history were one 24-hour day, our species appears about six seconds before midnight. Dinosaurs went extinct at 11:39 PM. The entire Industrial Revolution fits into the last five-thousandths of a second.
title: Human Age

insight.big: A rare stretch of stable climate — and one species changes the planet.
signs: Unusually steady for about 11,700 years — the calm in which farming and cities arose.
Rose about 120 m as the ice melted, drowning the land bridges; roughly stable for the last 7,000 years.
From a few million at the dawn of farming to more than 8 billion.
280 parts per million before industry. More than 420 now.
insight.know: Written records, tree rings, corals, lake mud and ice cores overlap, so many events of the last few thousand years can be dated to the exact year.
insight.today: Geologists proposed naming a new epoch, the Anthropocene, for the human era. In 2024 the international body that decides voted the formal proposal down — but the word, and the question behind it, have stuck.

ext.name: A sixth mass extinction?
ext.toll: Not yet on the scale of the Big Five — but species are being lost at an estimated tens to hundreds of times the natural rate
ext.cause: Habitat loss, over-hunting and over-fishing, invasive species, pollution and climate change. The dodo (last seen 1662), the passenger pigeon (1914) and the thylacine (1936) are on this map.
